Meat Temperature & Cooking Time Calculator

Cook steaks, roasts and chops to 145 °F and rest 3 minutes, ground meat to 160 °F, and all poultry to 165 °F. Always check with a thermometer; times are only estimates.

Unit

—

Safe minimum internal temperatures

From the USDA chart on FoodSafety.gov
FoodInternal temperatureRest time
Beef, pork, lamb, veal: steaks, roasts, chops145 °F (63 °C)3 minutes
Ground beef, pork, lamb, veal; sausage160 °F (71 °C)None
Poultry: whole, pieces and ground (chicken, turkey, duck)165 °F (74 °C)None
Ham, fresh (raw)145 °F (63 °C)3 minutes
Ham, fully cooked, to reheat140 °F (60 °C) if packaged in a USDA-inspected plant; otherwise 165 °F (74 °C)None
Fish145 °F (63 °C), or until the flesh is opaque and flakes easilyNone

Source: FoodSafety.gov safe minimum internal temperature chart (USDA). Always use a food thermometer.

RoastTimeNote

How it works

Pick what you're cooking and the calculator shows the safe internal temperature and rest time from the USDA chart. For roasts, enter the weight and it multiplies by the minutes per pound in the table above to give a time range at 325 °F. Steaks, chops, burgers and fish depend on thickness rather than weight, so for those it only gives the temperature. It all runs in your browser. Nothing you type is sent anywhere or saved.

Where to put the thermometer

In the thickest part of the meat, not touching bone, fat or the pan. For a whole bird, that's the innermost part of the thigh. Check a large roast in a couple of places.

Ways to use it

  • Roasting a chicken. 165 °F in the thigh, about 20 minutes per pound.
  • Checking a steak. 145 °F, then rest 3 minutes.
  • A pork roast. 145 °F is safe, and still a little pink in the middle.
  • Reheating ham. 140 °F for a store-bought cooked ham.
  • Grilling burgers. Ground meat needs 160 °F, more than a steak.

Questions

Why does steak rest but ground beef doesn’t need to?

On a whole steak or roast, germs are on the surface, and the 3-minute rest lets the heat keep working through the meat. Grinding mixes the surface into the middle, so ground meat has to reach a higher temperature, 160 °F, all the way through instead.

Is 145 °F safe for pork?

Yes. The USDA lowered the safe temperature for whole cuts of pork to 145 °F with a 3-minute rest. It may still look slightly pink, and that’s fine. Ground pork needs 160 °F.

Why is chicken 165 °F?

Poultry can carry salmonella throughout the meat, not just on the surface. At 165 °F those bacteria are killed almost instantly, so no rest time is needed for safety.

Can I trust the time alone?

No. Oven temperatures, pan sizes and how cold the meat was when it went in all change the time. Use the estimate to plan, and a thermometer to decide when it’s done.

Where do I put the thermometer?

In the thickest part, not touching bone, which conducts heat and reads high. For whole poultry, check the innermost part of the thigh and the thickest part of the breast.
